japa
(‘repetition [of the मन्त्र]’)
------------------------------------------
Japa has been an integral part of Hindu religious practices even from the Vedic days. Ceremonial repetition of Vedic passages has been a part and parcel of not only the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् but also other, post-Vedic, rituals.
Derived from the root-verb jap (‘to utter’) ‘japa’ means uttering or repetition of mantras (sacred passages or esoteric syllables or the names of deities of the Hindu pantheon). The word is sometimes defined as that which destroys sins and puts an end to rebirth (ja = janmanāśaka, destroyer of future birth; pa = pāpanāśaka, destroyer of sins).
The Bhagavadgītā (10.25) considers जप as one of the special manifestations of the Lord.
The जप of a मन्त्र can be practised in three different ways. When it is uttered loudly it is ‘vācika’ or ‘vaikharī’. If done inaudibly (like whispering) it is ‘upāṁśu’. If done mentally it is ‘mānasika’.
There are several classifications of जप:
nityajapa—that which is done regularly everyday like the Gāyatrījapa.
naimittikajapa—that which is done on special occasions like the periods of eclipses or festivals like शिवरात्रि.
kāmyajapa—that which is done for the fulfilment of desires like regaining health or earning wealth.
prāyaścittajapa—that which is done as an expiation for sins.
ajapājapa—that in which the process of breathing is coupled with the हṁस-मन्त्र (‘so’ham haṁsaḥ’). This is called ‘haṁsajapa’ also.
vilomajapa—that in which the मन्त्र is repeated in the reverse order. For e.g., repeating ‘namas’ śivāya’ as ‘ya vā śśi ma na’. This is generally done in countering black-magical rites.
likhitajapa—that in which the मन्त्र is written.
This is common even now. However, it should be done observing silence and with devotion.
Japa should be practised in a clean and quiet place, sitting erect on a comfortable seat. It should be done at a medium speed.
Before beginning the जप of a मन्त्र, the disciple is advised to remember gratefully the ṛṣi (the original sage to whom the मन्त्र was revealed), the छन्दस् (the meter) and the devatā (the deity). This must be followed by nyāsas (ceremonial purification of the hands and the limbs) and the dhyānaśloka (a verse that describes the form of the deity). After the जप is over, there must be japasamarpaṇa (offering the fruits of the जप to the deity itself).
A जपमाला (rosary) can be used for counting. Counting can be done on the fingers also.
See also DHYĀNA, DHYĀNAYOGA, JAPAMĀLĀ and MANTRA.

japamālā
(‘rosary, [used for] जप [or repetition of मन्त्र]’)
------------------------------------------
Repetition of a sacred formula or a divine name, especially in a ceremonial manner, is a part and parcel of many a religious practice. Such repetition, generally done mentally, is called ‘japa’. (See JAPA for more details.)
Japa must be practised, keeping the count, either on the fingers or with a जपमाला (a rosary). Hindu scriptural works prescribe many rules for its preparation and use.
Rudrākṣa (Elaescarpus ganitrus) beads, beads prepared out of dried sticks of the तुलसी (holy basil) plant or of dried wood of बिल्व (Aegle marmolos), gold, certain precious stones (crystal or quartz, coral, ruby, emerald and so on), beads of भस्म or dried holy ash—these are the materials used for preparing the जप-mālās. For stringing the beads, cotton or silk thread, wire of copper or silver, are used.
The number of beads should be 108, or 54 (and rarely 27). Sometimes it may be 64 or 32 also.
Japamālās made of different materials are prescribed for different mantras. For instance, the रुद्राक्ष beads are used by the Śaivas and Śāktas who repeat mantras connected with शिव or देवी. Mālās of तुलसी beads are used by the worshippers of विष्णु.
Sometimes different types of mālās are prescribed for getting different results. If mālās of रुद्राक्ष beads can give मोक्ष, those of pearls give competence in the knowledge of all sciences.
Generally, one bead will be extra in a mālā and that will be strung separately so as to stand like a crown. This is called ‘meru’. While counting, this मेरु should not be crossed. And, for counting on the mālā, the thumb should be used, supporting the mālā on the middle finger.
See also AKṢAMĀLĀ.
